claim: Mutations in TIMM8A cause Mohr-Tranebjærg syndrome (MTS), which is characterized by sensorineural hearing loss, dystonia and blindness.
source: Mutations in TIMM8A cause a neurodegenerative disease, Mohr-Tranebjærg syndrome (MTS), which is characterised by sensorineural hearing loss, dystonia and blindness.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is supported by citations in the introduction (Jin et al., 1996; Koehler et al., 1999; Tranebjaerg et al., 1995).

claim: hTim8a is required for the assembly of Complex IV in neurons.
source: We show that hTim8a is required for the assembly of Complex IV in neurons, which is mediated through a transient interaction with Complex IV assembly factors, in particular the copper chaperone COX17.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data including proteomics (Figure 2), BN-PAGE analysis (Figure 6), and immunoprecipitation experiments (Figure 7).

claim: Complex IV assembly defects resulting from loss of hTim8a lead to oxidative stress.
source: Complex IV assembly defects resulting from loss of hTim8a leads to oxidative stress and changes to key apoptotic regulators, including cytochrome c, which primes cells for death.
evidence: This is supported by ROS measurements shown in Figure 8A and respiratory chain activity measurements in Figure 4F.

claim: Loss of hTim8a leads to changes in key apoptotic regulators including cytochrome c.
source: Complex IV assembly defects resulting from loss of hTim8a leads to oxidative stress and changes to key apoptotic regulators, including cytochrome c, which primes cells for death.
evidence: This is demonstrated by western blot analysis in Figure 3A and F showing increased cytochrome c levels.

claim: Alleviation of oxidative stress with Vitamin E treatment rescues cells from apoptotic vulnerability.
source: Alleviation of oxidative stress with Vitamin E treatment rescues cells from apoptotic vulnerability.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 8C and D showing reduced cytochrome c levels and decreased apoptotic sensitivity following Vitamin E treatment.

claim: Enhanced sensitivity of neuronal cells to apoptosis is the underlying mechanism of MTS.
source: We hypothesise that enhanced sensitivity of neuronal cells to apoptosis is the underlying mechanism of MTS.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the experimental findings showing increased apoptotic sensitivity in hTim8a-deficient cells.

claim: Human cells have six small TIM proteins: hTim8a, hTim8b, hTim9, hTim10a, hTim10b, and hTim13.
source: human cells have six small TIM proteins that have been poorly characterised, these include, hTim8a, hTim8b, hTim9, hTim10a, hTim10b, and hTim13 (Bauer et al., 1999; Gentle et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: Yeast have five well-characterized small TIM proteins: Tim8, Tim9, Tim10, Tim12 and Tim13.
source: Unlike yeast that have five well-characterised small TIM proteins, Tim8, Tim9, Tim10, Tim12 and Tim13 (Koehler, 2004; Koehler et al., 1999; Koehler et al., 1998)
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: hTim8a is predominantly expressed in brain.
source: the predominate expression of hTim8a in brain (Jin et al., 1999), suggests cell specific functions.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Jin et al., 1999.

claim: Mutations in TIMM8A cause an X-linked recessive neurodegenerative disorder.
source: mutations in the TIMM8A gene that encodes the hTim8a protein, cause Mohr-Tranebjærg syndrome (MTS), an X-linked recessive neurodegenerative disorder characterised by progressive sensorineural hearing loss, dystonia, cortical blindness and dysphagia (Jin et al., 1996; Koehler et al., 1999; Tranebjaerg et al., 1995).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: Defects in the import of human Tim23 have been assumed to be the underlying basis of MTS.
source: Given the function of yeast Tim8 in the import of Tim23, it has been assumed that defects in the import of human Tim23 were the underlying basis of MTS (Leuenberger et al., 1999; Paschen et al., 2000; Rothbauer et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated as a previous assumption in the literature with supporting citations.

claim: hTim9MUT cells show reduced steady state levels of TIM22 complex subunits (hTim22 and Tim29).
source: Mitochondria isolated from hTim9MUT cells show reduced steady state levels of TIM22 complex subunits (hTim22 and Tim29) and substrates of the TIM22 complex (ANT3, GC1 and hTim23) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A)
evidence: This is demonstrated by western blot analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: hTim9MUT cells display severe assembly defects of the TIM22 complex.
source: displayed severe assembly defects of the TIM22 complex (Figure 1A, compare lanes 3 and 4).
evidence: This is demonstrated by BN-PAGE analysis shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Lack of functional hTim8a in both HEK293 and SH-SY5Y cells had no obvious impact on the TIM22 complex or TIM22 substrates when analyzed by SDS-PAGE.
source: To the contrary, lack of functional hTim8a in both HEK293 and SH-SY5Y cells had no obvious impact on the TIM22 complex or TIM22 substrates when analysed by SDS-PAGE (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A)
evidence: This is demonstrated by western blot analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Lack of functional hTim8a in both HEK293 and SH-SY5Y cells had no obvious impact on the TIM22 complex when analyzed by BN-PAGE.
source: lack of functional hTim8a in both HEK293 and SH-SY5Y cells had no obvious impact on the TIM22 complex or TIM22 substrates when analysed by SDS-PAGE (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A) or BN-PAGE (Figure 1B and C; quantified for hTim8aMUT SH in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by BN-PAGE analysis shown in Figures 1B and 1C.

claim: Depletion of hTim8b in HEK293 or SH-SY5Y cells had minimal impact on the levels of the TIM22 or TIM23 complex.
source: Likewise, depletion of hTim8b in HEK293 or SH-SY5Y cells had minimal impact on the levels of the TIM22 or TIM23 complex (Figure 1D and E; Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by BN-PAGE and western blot analysis shown in Figures 1D, 1E, and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: In vitro mitochondrial import assays suggest no defects in the assembly of hTim23, hTim22, and GC1 in hTim8aKO and hTim8bKO cells.
source: Further analysis using in vitro mitochondrial import assays of [35S]-hTim23, [35S]-hTim22 and the glutamate carrier ([35S]-GC1) into mitochondria isolated from hTim8aKO and hTim8bKO (Figure 1F–H) or hTim8aMUT SH cells (Figure 1I) suggests no defects in the assembly of these putative substrates.
evidence: This is demonstrated by import assays shown in Figures 1F-I.

claim: hTim9 is firmly embedded in the TIM22 complex biogenesis pathway, like its yeast counterpart.
source: This data demonstrates that hTim9 is firmly embedded in the TIM22 complex biogenesis pathway, like its yeast counterpart
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing severe TIM22 complex defects in hTim9MUT cells.

claim: hTim8a and hTim8b do not directly influence the TIM22 complex or pathway and may have alternative function(s) within human mitochondria.
source: while hTim8a and hTim8b do not directly influence the TIM22 complex or pathway and may have alternative function(s) within human mitochondria.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of TIM22 complex defects in cells lacking hTim8a or hTim8b.

claim: The normal import and assembly of hTim23 in the absence of hTim8a and hTim8b suggests there is an alternative pathomechanism underlying MTS.
source: The normal import and assembly of hTim23 in the absence of hTim8a and hTim8b suggests there is an alternative pathomechanism underlying MTS.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing normal hTim23 import in cells lacking hTim8a or hTim8b.

claim: hTim8aKO mitochondria showed a decrease in the levels of hTim13 and hTim8b.
source: hTim8aKO mitochondria showed a decrease in the levels of: (i) hTim13 and hTim8b; (ii) the Apoptosis Inducing Factor, AIF; (iii) the Complex IV assembly factor, COX17; and (iv) two proteins belonging to the SLC25 family, SLC25A5 (ANT2) and SLC25A14, a previously described mitochondrial uncoupling protein (UCP5) (Kim-Han et al., 2001; Sanchis et al., 1998; Figure 2B and Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative mass spectrometry shown in Figure 2B.

claim: hTim8aKO mitochondria showed a decrease in the levels of the Apoptosis Inducing Factor (AIF).
source: hTim8aKO mitochondria showed a decrease in the levels of: (i) hTim13 and hTim8b; (ii) the Apoptosis Inducing Factor, AIF; (iii) the Complex IV assembly factor, COX17; and (iv) two proteins belonging to the SLC25 family, SLC25A5 (ANT2) and SLC25A14, a previously described mitochondrial uncoupling protein (UCP5) (Kim-Han et al., 2001; Sanchis et al., 1998; Figure 2B and Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative mass spectrometry shown in Figure 2B.

claim: hTim8aKO mitochondria showed a decrease in the levels of the Complex IV assembly factor COX17.
source: hTim8aKO mitochondria showed a decrease in the levels of: (i) hTim13 and hTim8b; (ii) the Apoptosis Inducing Factor, AIF; (iii) the Complex IV assembly factor, COX17; and (iv) two proteins belonging to the SLC25 family, SLC25A5 (ANT2) and SLC25A14, a previously described mitochondrial uncoupling protein (UCP5) (Kim-Han et al., 2001; Sanchis et al., 1998; Figure 2B and Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative mass spectrometry shown in Figure 2B.

claim: hTim8aKO cells displayed upregulated levels of the pro-apoptotic BCL-2 family member Bax.
source: hTim8aKO cells also displayed upregulated levels of the pro-apoptotic BCL-2 family member Bax.
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative mass spectrometry shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The absence of hTim8a in SH-SY5Y cells showed reduced levels of mitochondrially-encoded COX2 (MT-CO2) and COX3 (MT-CO3).
source: The absence of hTim8a in SH-SY5Y cells (Figure 2C and Figure 2—source data 1), showed a strikingly different profile to the HEK293 cells with changes to both mitochondrial and nuclear encoded Complex IV subunits and assembly factors. Specifically, reduced levels of mitochondrially-encoded COX2 (MT-CO2) and COX3 (MT-CO3) and nuclear-encoded COX6A1, COX6C and COX7A2 were observed
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative mass spectrometry shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The absence of hTim8a in SH-SY5Y cells showed reduced levels of nuclear-encoded COX6A1, COX6C and COX7A2.
source: The absence of hTim8a in SH-SY5Y cells (Figure 2C and Figure 2—source data 1), showed a strikingly different profile to the HEK293 cells with changes to both mitochondrial and nuclear encoded Complex IV subunits and assembly factors. Specifically, reduced levels of mitochondrially-encoded COX2 (MT-CO2) and COX3 (MT-CO3) and nuclear-encoded COX6A1, COX6C and COX7A2 were observed
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative mass spectrometry shown in Figure 2C.

claim: In hTim8aMUT SH cells, COX17 was down-regulated and two putative assembly factors COA5 and COX15 were upregulated.
source: while COX17 was down-regulated and two putative assembly factors COA5 and COX15, were upregulated.
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative mass spectrometry shown in Figure 2C.

claim: hTim8bKO HEK293 cells showed reduced levels in Complex IV assembly factors including COX17, COA4, COA5, COA7 and CMC4.
source: Indeed, hTim8bKO HEK293 cells showed reduced levels in Complex IV assembly factors including COX17, COA4, COA5, COA7 and CMC4 (Figure 2D and Figure 2—source data 1)
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative mass spectrometry shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Depletion of hTim8b in SH-SY5Y cells led to changes to both mitochondrial and nuclear encoded Complex IV subunits and assembly factors.
source: while depletion of hTim8b in SH-SY5Y cells also led to changes to both mitochondrial and nuclear encoded Complex IV subunits and assembly factors (Figure 2E and Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative mass spectrometry shown in Figure 2E.

claim: hTim8a and hTim8b have a role in the biogenesis of Complex IV.
source: Taken together this data suggest a role of hTim8a and hTim8b in the biogenesis of Complex IV.
evidence: This is inferred from the proteomics data showing changes in Complex IV subunits and assembly factors.

claim: HEK293 cells lacking hTim8a show down-regulation of AIF and upregulation of Bax.
source: A change that caught our attention in the proteomics data was the up and down-regulation of key apoptotic regulators in HEK293 cells lacking hTim8a, including down-regulation of the Apoptosis Inducting Factor (AIF) and upregulation in the pro-apoptotic Bax.
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative mass spectrometry shown in Figure 2B and confirmed by western blot in Figure 3A.

claim: Changes to AIF and Bax were not evident in hTim9MUT or hTim8bKO mitochondria.
source: Changes to AIF and Bax were not evident in hTim9MUT or hTim8bKO mitochondria, suggesting a specific cellular response due to the lack of hTim8a and a potential increased susceptibility to apoptosis.
evidence: This is inferred from the proteomics data shown in Figures 2A and 2D.

claim: hTim8aKO cells show an upregulation in the levels of cytochrome c.
source: We confirmed changes to the levels of AIF and Bax by western blot and also uncovered an upregulation in the levels of cytochrome c (Figure 3A, compare lanes 1 and 2 and quantification).
evidence: This is demonstrated by western blot analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Changes in Bax, cytochrome c, and AIF were not apparent in hTim8bKO mitochondria.
source: These changes were not apparent in hTim8bKO mitochondria (Figure 3A, lanes 3 and 4 and quantification)
evidence: This is demonstrated by western blot analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Complementation with hTim8a restored the steady-state protein levels of Bax, cytochrome c and AIF in hTim8aKO cells.
source: and were not off-target effects, as complementation with hTim8a (hTim8aKO+WT) restored the steady-state protein levels of Bax, cytochrome c and AIF (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by western blot analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Alterations in the abundance of cytochrome c and Bax in hTim8aKO cells were not due to large changes in their gene expression as measured by qPCR.
source: Alterations in the abundance of cytochrome c and Bax were not due to large changes in their gene expression as measured by qPCR, while the impact on AIF was due to transcriptional regulation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by qPCR analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The impact on AIF in hTim8aKO cells was due to transcriptional regulation.
source: Alterations in the abundance of cytochrome c and Bax were not due to large changes in their gene expression as measured by qPCR, while the impact on AIF was due to transcriptional regulation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by qPCR analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Treatment of control and hTim8aKO cells with staurosporine induced a faster release of cytochrome c from mitochondria in hTim8aKO cells.
source: Treatment of control and hTim8aKO cells with staurosporine (STS), induced a faster release of cytochrome c from mitochondria in hTim8aKO cells (Figure 3C), suggesting these cells were more sensitive to apoptotic induction.
evidence: This is demonstrated by western blot analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: hTim8aKO cells show a higher frequency of death following STS treatment compared to control cells.
source: Indeed, when we measured the rate of apoptotic induction in control, hTim8aKO and hTim8bKO cells we noted a higher frequency of death following STS treatment only in cells lacking hTim8a (Figure 3D; shown as % of cell death in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by apoptosis assays shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The rate of apoptosis was significantly increased in hTim8aKO cells when challenged with ABT-737.
source: To test if loss of hTim8a specifically leads to mitochondrial-mediated apoptotic cell death, control, hTim8aKO and hTim8bKO cells were challenged with ABT-737, a BH3 mimetic inhibitor of Bcl-xL, Bcl-2 and Bcl-w and the rate of apoptosis was significantly increased in hTim8aKO cells and only slightly in cells lacking hTim8b (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by apoptosis assays shown in Figure 3E.

claim: HEK293 cells lacking hTim8a are in a primed for cell death state.
source: We propose that HEK293 cells lacking hTim8a are in a primed for cell death state such that they can undergo a rapid death following cellular insult.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the apoptosis sensitivity data.

claim: Mitochondria isolated from hTim8aMUT SH cells had a similar increase in the level of cytochrome c relative to control cells.
source: Mitochondria isolated from hTim8aMUT SH cells had a similar increase in the level of cytochrome c relative to control cells, but only modest changes in the steady-state levels of AIF and Bax were observed (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by western blot analysis shown in Figure 3F.

claim: hTim8aMUT SH cells were more vulnerable to STS-induced apoptosis compared to control cells.
source: hTim8aMUT SH cells were also more vulnerable to STS-induced apoptosis compared to control cells (Figure 3G)
evidence: This is demonstrated by apoptosis assays shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Treatment with ABT-737 increased the rate of apoptosis in hTim8aMUT SH cells.
source: and treatment with ABT-737 also increased the rate of apoptosis in these cells. These effects were reversed when cells were pre-treated with a broad-spectrum caspase inhibitor QVD-OPh (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by apoptosis assays shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Pre-treatment with QVD-OPh reversed the increased apoptosis in hTim8aMUT SH cells treated with ABT-737.
source: These effects were reversed when cells were pre-treated with a broad-spectrum caspase inhibitor QVD-OPh (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by apoptosis assays shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Increased caspase-3 cleavage was observed in hTim8aMUT SH cells when treated with STS or ABT-737.
source: In agreement with this, we observed increased caspase-3 cleavage in hTim8aMUT SH cells when treated with STS or ABT-737. Caspase-3 processing was completely inhibited in the presence of QVD-OPh (Figure 3I, compare lanes 6 and 8 to 10 and 12), consistent with the inhibition of apoptosis.
evidence: This is demonstrated by western blot analysis shown in Figure 3I.

claim: Caspase-3 processing was completely inhibited in the presence of QVD-OPh in hTim8aMUT SH cells.
source: Caspase-3 processing was completely inhibited in the presence of QVD-OPh (Figure 3I, compare lanes 6 and 8 to 10 and 12), consistent with the inhibition of apoptosis.
evidence: This is demonstrated by western blot analysis shown in Figure 3I.

claim: Treatment with specific ferroptosis inducers did not enhance cell death of hTim8aMUT SH cells.
source: We also examined whether loss of hTim8a increased vulnerability to ferroptosis (Dixon et al., 2012; Simon et al., 2000; Wu et al., 2018), but treatment with specific ferroptosis inducers, including: (i) Erastin, an SLC7A11 inhibitor; (ii) (1S,3R)-RSL3, which inhibits glutathione peroxidase four and (iii) buthionine sulfoximine (BSO), which depletes glutathione (GSH), did not enhance cell death of hTim8aMUT SH cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by cell viability assays shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Loss of hTim8a sensitises cells to Bcl-2-regulated and caspase-dependent, intrinsic cell death.
source: Thus, we conclude that loss of hTim8a sensitises cells to Bcl-2-regulated and caspase-dependent, intrinsic cell death.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the apoptosis sensitivity data with ABT-737 and QVD-OPh.

claim: HEK293 cells lacking hTim8b were less viable than HEK293 cells lacking hTim8a.
source: Cell viability measured using trypan blue staining revealed HEK293 cells lacking hTim8b were less viable than HEK293 cells lacking hTim8a, while SH-SY5Y cells lacking hTim8a (hTim8aMUT SH)were significantly less viable than control and hTim8bKO SH cells (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by cell viability assays shown in Figure 4A.

claim: SH-SY5Y cells lacking hTim8a were significantly less viable than control and hTim8bKO SH cells.
source: Cell viability measured using trypan blue staining revealed HEK293 cells lacking hTim8b were less viable than HEK293 cells lacking hTim8a, while SH-SY5Y cells lacking hTim8a (hTim8aMUT SH)were significantly less viable than control and hTim8bKO SH cells (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by cell viability assays shown in Figure 4A.

claim: HEK293 cells lacking hTim8a have compromised membrane potential.
source: Incubation of cells with the membrane potential indicator, TMRM, indicated compromised membrane potential in HEK293 cells lacking hTim8a, but a more severe defect in cells lacking hTim8b (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by TMRM uptake assays shown in Figure 4B.

claim: HEK293 cells lacking hTim8b have a more severe membrane potential defect than cells lacking hTim8a.
source: Incubation of cells with the membrane potential indicator, TMRM, indicated compromised membrane potential in HEK293 cells lacking hTim8a, but a more severe defect in cells lacking hTim8b (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by TMRM uptake assays shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Loss of hTim8b in SH-SY5Y cells had no impact on the mitochondrial membrane potential.
source: Interestingly, loss of hTim8b in SH-SY5Y cells had no impact on the mitochondrial membrane potential, while those cells lacking functional hTim8a had a significant defect (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by TMRM uptake assays shown in Figure 4B.

claim: SH-SY5Y cells lacking functional hTim8a had a significant mitochondrial membrane potential defect.
source: Interestingly, loss of hTim8b in SH-SY5Y cells had no impact on the mitochondrial membrane potential, while those cells lacking functional hTim8a had a significant defect (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by TMRM uptake assays shown in Figure 4B.

claim: HEK293 cells lacking hTim8a or hTim8b show no respiration defect.
source: Oxygen consumption rate (OCR) measurements (Figure 4C–4E), suggested no respiration defect in HEK293 cells lacking hTim8a or hTim8b, however a minor reduction in maximal OCR in hTim8bKO HEK293 following the addition of FCCP was observed (Figure 4C and D, left panel).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Seahorse OCR measurements shown in Figures 4C-E.

claim: A minor reduction in maximal OCR in hTim8bKO HEK293 following the addition of FCCP was observed.
source: Oxygen consumption rate (OCR) measurements (Figure 4C–4E), suggested no respiration defect in HEK293 cells lacking hTim8a or hTim8b, however a minor reduction in maximal OCR in hTim8bKO HEK293 following the addition of FCCP was observed (Figure 4C and D, left panel).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Seahorse OCR measurements shown in Figures 4C and D.

claim: The extracellular acidification rate (ECAR) was significantly affected in HEK293 cells lacking either hTim8a or hTim8b.
source: The extracellular acidification rate (ECAR) was significantly affected in the HEK293 lacking either hTim8a or hTim8b expression suggesting perturbations to glycolysis in these cells (Figure 4D, left panel).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Seahorse ECAR measurements shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The OCR of hTim8aMUT SH was significantly compromised compared to control SH-SY5Y cells.
source: The OCR of hTim8aMUT SH was significantly compromised compared to control SH-SY5Y cells (Figure 4C, right panel).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Seahorse OCR measurements shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Both the basal and maximal respiration rates of hTim8aMUT SH were more severely impaired than hTim8bKO SH.
source: Both the basal and maximal respiration rates of hTim8aMUT SH were more severely impaired than hTim8bKO SH(58% versus 78% of control; 60% versus 92% of control; Figure 4D, right panel).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Seahorse OCR measurements shown in Figure 4D.

claim: No defect in respiratory chain activity was observed in hTim8aKO or hTim8bKO HEK293 cells.
source: In agreement with the OCR measurements on HEK293 cells, we observed no defect in respiratory chain activity in hTim8aKO or hTim8bKO HEK293 cells (Figure 4F, left panel)
evidence: This is demonstrated by respiratory chain enzyme activity assays shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Respiratory complex activities seemed slightly upregulated in hTim8aKO HEK293, possibly to compensate for defective glycolysis.
source: instead respiratory complex activities seemed slightly upregulated in hTim8aKO HEK293, possibly to compensate for defective glycolysis observed in these cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the respiratory chain enzyme activity data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: hTim8aMUT SH or hTim8bKO SH cells exhibited significant defects in the activities of Complex I and IV.
source: In contrast, the hTim8aMUT SH or hTim8bKO SH cells exhibited significant defects in the activities of Complex I and IV (55% and 67% of control; 64% and 81% of control), in agreement with the proteomics analyses showing clear defects on Complex IV biogenesis accompanied with mild defect in Complex I.
evidence: This is demonstrated by respiratory chain enzyme activity assays shown in Figure 4F.

claim: hTim8b has a more prominent function in HEK293 cells, while the function of hTim8a is more important in the neuronal like SH-SY5Y cell line.
source: This data suggests that hTim8b has a more prominent function in HEK293 cells, while the function of hTim8a is more important in the neuronal like SH-SY5Y cell line.
evidence: This is inferred from the cell viability, membrane potential, and respiratory chain activity data.

claim: Fifty-nine metabolites were significantly altered in hTim8aKO cells compared to control HEK293 cells.
source: Fifty-nine of these metabolites were significantly altered (BH-adjusted p<0.05) in hTim8aKO cells suggesting a distinct metabolomic footprint compared to control HEK293 cells (Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by metabolomics analysis.

claim: hTim8aKO cells show significant changes in central carbon metabolism, indicated by decreases in the levels of TCA cycle intermediates.
source: Analysis of detected metabolites depicted as a heatmap with the top 40 most-significantly altered metabolites or as a pathway map (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), suggested significant changes in central carbon metabolism in hTim8aKO cells, indicated by decreases in the levels of TCA cycle intermediates (including citrate, fumarate, malate), decreases in intermediates in lower glycolysis (DHAP, GAP, 2/3PGA, lactate) and a concomitant increase in intermediates in upper glycolysis and the pentose phosphate pathway (glucose, Glc6P, Rib5P, Ru5P).
evidence: This is demonstrated by metabolomics analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: hTim8aKO cells show decreases in intermediates in lower glycolysis and a concomitant increase in intermediates in upper glycolysis and the pentose phosphate pathway.
source: Analysis of detected metabolites depicted as a heatmap with the top 40 most-significantly altered metabolites or as a pathway map (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), suggested significant changes in central carbon metabolism in hTim8aKO cells, indicated by decreases in the levels of TCA cycle intermediates (including citrate, fumarate, malate), decreases in intermediates in lower glycolysis (DHAP, GAP, 2/3PGA, lactate) and a concomitant increase in intermediates in upper glycolysis and the pentose phosphate pathway (glucose, Glc6P, Rib5P, Ru5P).
evidence: This is demonstrated by metabolomics analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Loss of hTim8a leads to specific defects in mitochondrial metabolism and alterations of non-mitochondrial pathways of central carbon metabolism in HEK293 cells.
source: Loss of hTim8a therefore, leads to specific defects in mitochondrial metabolism and alterations of non-mitochondrial pathways of central carbon metabolism in HEK293 cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the metabolomics data.

claim: The metabolic response of SH-SY5Y cells to loss of hTim8a differed from that of hTim8aKO HEK293 cells.
source: Metabolite profiling indicated that the metabolic response of SH-SY5Y cells to loss of hTim8a, differed from that of hTim8aKO HEK293 cells (Figure 5A and B; Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by metabolomics analysis shown in Figures 5A, 5B, and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Levels of many intermediates of the TCA cycle and interconnected pathways were significantly elevated in hTim8aMUT SH cells.
source: In particular, levels of many intermediates of the TCA cycle (citrate/isocitrate, fumarate, succinate) and interconnected pathways (glutamine) were significantly elevated, rather than reduced, in the hTim8aMUT SH cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by metabolomics analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Both malate and aspartate were significantly reduced in hTim8aMUT SH cells.
source: Both malate and aspartate were significantly reduced in hTim8aMUT SH cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 2), and the malate-aspartate shuttle is the most affected pathway in hTim8aMUT SH cells (Figure 5B)
evidence: This is demonstrated by metabolomics analysis shown in Figures 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The malate-aspartate shuttle is the most affected pathway in hTim8aMUT SH cells.
source: Both malate and aspartate were significantly reduced in hTim8aMUT SH cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 2), and the malate-aspartate shuttle is the most affected pathway in hTim8aMUT SH cells (Figure 5B)
evidence: This is demonstrated by metabolomics pathway analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: hTim8aMUT SH cells had a significant accumulation of epinephrine and changes in multiple metabolite intermediates of catecholamine pathway.
source: hTim8aMUT SH cells also had a significant accumulation of epinephrine and changes in multiple metabolite intermediates of catecholamine pathway (metabolites/pathway coloured in pink in Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by metabolomics analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The catabolism of 13C-glucose and 13C-glutamine was highly compartmentalized in both control and hTim8aMUT SH cell lines.
source: The catabolism of 13C-glucose and 13C-glutamine was highly compartmentalized in both cell lines, with 13C-glucose being catabolized via glycolysis to lactate, and 13C-glutamine being primarily catabolized in the TCA cycle (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by 13C-labeling experiments shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Levels of 13C-enrichment in different intermediates in the two 13C-glucose labelled cell lines were similar, with the exception of glycerol-3-phosphate.
source: Levels of 13C-enrichment in different intermediates in the two 13C-glucose labelled cell lines were similar, with the exception of glycerol-3-phosphate, which was more highly labelled in hTim8aMUT SH (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by 13C-labeling experiments shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Levels of 13C-enrichment in intermediates in the oxidative TCA cycle were decreased by ~30% in hTim8aMUT SH cells compared to control cells.
source: While levels of uptake of 13C-glutamine were not affected in the Tim8aMUT SH cells (indicated by labelling levels of 5-oxoproline), levels of 13C-enrichment in intermediates in the oxidative TCA cycle, starting from α-ketoglutarate (as reflected in glutamate labelling) to malate/oxaloacetic acid were decreased by ~30% compared to control cells (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by 13C-labeling experiments shown in Figure 5C.

claim: 13C-enrichment in citric acid was almost completely repressed in the 13C-glutamine-fed hTim8aMUT cells.
source: Strikingly, 13C-enrichment in citric acid was almost completely repressed in the 13C-glutamine-fed hTim8aMUT cells, indicating that most or all of the oxaloacetate produced in the mitochondria is exported to the cytosol as part of the malate-aspartate shuttle.
evidence: This is demonstrated by 13C-labeling experiments shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Loss of hTim8a in SH-SY5Y cells leads to a decrease in the rate of utilization of glutamine.
source: Loss of hTim8a in SH-SY5Y cells therefore appears to lead to a decrease in the rate of utilization of glutamine, the major carbon source driving the mitochondrial TCA cycle and oxidative phosphorylation, leading to decreased production of malate and oxaloacetate and the pool of intermediates for the malate-aspartate shuttle.
evidence: This is inferred from the 13C-labeling experiments shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Loss of hTim8a in SH-SY5Y cells leads to dysregulation of mitochondrial metabolism and redox balance.
source: These analyses indicate that loss of hTim8a in SH-SY5Y cells leads to dysregulation of mitochondrial metabolism and redox balance, indicating a vital role in neuronal cell biology.
evidence: This is inferred from the metabolomics and 13C-labeling data.

claim: hTim8bKO HEK293, hTim8aMUT SH-SY5Y and hTim8bKO SH-SY5Y cells showed decreased abundance in Complex IV subunits or assembly factors compared to control cells.
source: A closer look at the quantitative mass-spectrometry data from all four knock-out cell lines highlighted the importance of hTim8a and hTim8b in maintenance of Complex IV subunits, especially in the SH-SY5Y neuronal cell model (Figure 6A and B). hTim8bKO HEK293, hTim8aMUT SH-SY5Y and hTim8bKO SH-SY5Y cells showed decreased abundance in Complex IV subunits or assembly factors compared to control cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative mass spectrometry shown in Figures 6A and 6B.

claim: hTim8aKO HEK293 did not show decreased abundance in Complex IV subunits or assembly factors.
source: hTim8aKO HEK293 did not share this phenotype, however this may reflect the tissue-specific expression and/or function of hTim8a.
evidence: This is inferred from the quantitative mass spectrometry data shown in Figures 6A and 6B.

claim: Loss of either hTim8a or hTim8b had minimal effect on SLC25A-family carrier proteins and TIM proteins.
source: Further support for a novel role of hTim8 proteins in Complex IV assembly comes from the minimal effect that loss of either hTim8a or hTim8b had on SLC25A-family carrier proteins and TIM proteins, those thought to be putative substrates based on work in yeast (Figure 6A, upper panel).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative mass spectrometry shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The OXPHOS defect in hTim8a and hTim8b deficient cells is specific to Complex IV.
source: By collating the relative abundance of subunits from each OXPHOS complex, it is clear the OXPHOS defect is not a generic OXPHOS defect or downregulation but specific to Complex IV (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative mass spectrometry shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Both hTim8aMUT SH and hTim8bKO SH-SY5Y cell lines had reduced protein levels for all core subunits of Complex IV.
source: Both hTim8aMUT SH and hTim8bKO SHSY5Y cell lines had reduced protein levels for all core subunits of Complex IV, a less severe reduction in the majority of Complex I subunits and little or no effect on Complexes II, III and V.
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative mass spectrometry shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The downward trend of Complex I in hTim8a and hTim8b deficient cells reflects a co-dependency of Complex I on Complex IV for stability in respiratory supercomplexes.
source: Despite the downward trend of Complex I as a whole, few individual subunits are depleted significantly (Figure 6A, middle panel) and we believe this reflects a co-dependency of Complex I on Complex IV for stability in respiratory supercomplexes (Li et al., 2007) not a direct influence of hTim8a or hTim8b on Complex I.
evidence: This is inferred from the mass spectrometry data and supported by a citation to Li et al., 2007.

claim: hTim8aKO HEK293 cells show little impact on Complex IV stability.
source: The latter supported the proteomic data, with hTim8aKO HEK293 cells showing little impact on Complex IV stability (Figure 6C)
evidence: This is demonstrated by BN-PAGE analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Mitochondria isolated from hTim8aMUT SH-SY5Y cells displayed reduced levels of Complex IV and preferential interaction of COX4 with a high MW intermediate.
source: while mitochondria isolated from control and hTim8aMUT SH-SY5Y cells displayed reduced levels of Complex IV (COX4 antibodies) and preferential interaction of COX4 with in a high MW intermediate (Figure 6D, upper panels) as has been seen in patients with mutations in genes encoding Complex IV assembly factors (Lazarou et al., 2009; Stroud et al., 2015).
evidence: This is demonstrated by BN-PAGE analysis shown in Figure 6D and supported by citations to Lazarou et al., 2009 and Stroud et al., 2015.

claim: Mitochondria from HEK293 cells lacking hTim8b showed reduced levels of monomeric Complex IV and preferential interaction of COX4 with a high MW intermediate.
source: Interestingly, mitochondria from HEK293 cells lacking hTim8b (hTim8bKO) showed a similar profile when probed with COX4 (Figure 6D, left panel), that is reduced levels of monomeric Complex IV and preferential interaction of COX4 with a high MW intermediate.
evidence: This is demonstrated by BN-PAGE analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The absence of hTim8b in SH-SY5Y cells had little impact on the Complex IV monomer.
source: However, the absence of hTim8b in the SH-SY5Y cells had little impact on the Complex IV monomer.
evidence: This is inferred from the BN-PAGE analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The data reinforces the cell specific functions of the hTim8 isoforms in Complex IV biology.
source: This data reinforces the cell specific functions of the hTim8 isoforms in Complex IV biology.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the differential effects of hTim8a and hTim8b loss in different cell types.

claim: There was a common impact on steady state levels of COX17 in all cell lines lacking either hTim8a or hTim8b.
source: In vitro mitochondrial import assays of a number of Complex IV subunits and assembly factors did not reveal any obvious defects or intermediates (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B and C), however we noted that there was a common impact on steady state levels of COX17 in all cells lines lacking either hTim8a or hTim8b (Figure 2 and Figure 2—source data 1)
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative mass spectrometry shown in Figure 2.

claim: A COX17-dependent process is being impacted in the absence of hTim8a and hTim8b.
source: and this suggested a COX17-dependent process was being impacted in the absence of hTim8a and hTim8b.
evidence: This is inferred from the common reduction in COX17 levels across all hTim8a and hTim8b deficient cell lines.

claim: SH-SY5Y cells depleted of hTim8a have reduced COX17 protein levels.
source: We confirmed the reduction in COX17 protein levels in SH-SY5Y cells depleted of hTim8a (Figure 7A)
evidence: This is demonstrated by western blot analysis shown in Figure 7A.

claim: [35S]-COX17 import into mitochondria isolated from hTim8aMUT and control SH-SY5Y cells showed normal kinetics by SDS-PAGE.
source: [35S]-COX17 import into mitochondria isolated from hTim8aMUT and control SH-SY5Y cells showed normal kinetics by SDS-PAGE (Figure 7B), which was expected given that COX17 is an established Mia40 substrate (Banci et al., 2010).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vitro import assays shown in Figure 7B and supported by a citation to Banci et al., 2010.

claim: Analysis of in vitro import reactions by BN-PAGE suggested that COX17 assembly was perturbed in the absence of hTim8a.
source: However, analysis of in vitro import reactions by BN-PAGE to monitor assembly of [35S]-COX17 did suggest that COX17 assembly was perturbed in the absence of hTim8a (Figure 7C;~40% less COX17 assembly compared to control).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vitro import assays analyzed by BN-PAGE shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Under standard IP conditions, no interaction between hTim8a and COX17 was captured.
source: hTim8aFLAG was re-expressed in hTim8aMUT SH cells and mitochondria were isolated from these cells for downstream immunoprecipitation (IP) using FLAG antibodies. Under these conditions no interaction between hTim8a and COX17 was captured (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Using crosslinking with DSP prior to immunoprecipitation, an interaction between hTim8aFLAG and COX17 was captured.
source: Using this approach, we captured an interaction between hTim8aFLAG and COX17 by western blotting (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by crosslinking and immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 7F.

claim: When grown in glucose-containing media, the most enriched interacting partners for hTim8a were hTim8b and hTim13, in addition to Complex IV assembly factors (Coa4 and Coa7) and one Complex IV subunit (Cox6B1).
source: When grown in glucose-containing media the most enriched interacting partners for hTim8a were hTim8b and hTim13, in addition to Complex IV assembly factors (Coa4 and Coa7) and one Complex IV subunit (Cox6B1) (Figure 7G and Figure 7—source data 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by crosslinking/IP followed by mass spectrometry shown in Figure 7G.

claim: Under high respiratory demand (galactose), hTim13 is one of the least enriched partners of hTim8a, while there is a corresponding enrichment of Complex IV assembly factors and subunits.
source: This profile changes under high respiratory demand and hTim13 is one of the least enriched partners, while a corresponding enrichment of Complex IV assembly factors (COA4, COA6, COA7) and subunits (COX6B1 and COX4l1), in addition to cytochrome c is observed (Figure 7G, right panel; Figure 7—source data 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by crosslinking/IP followed by mass spectrometry shown in Figure 7G.

claim: Under high respiratory demand, key players of mitochondrial quality control pathways, pGAM5, OPA1, YME1L and the Prohibitins were enriched as hTim8a interacting partners.
source: Additionally enriched proteins included key players of mitochondrial quality control pathways, pGAM5, OPA1, YME1L and the Prohibitins.
evidence: This is demonstrated by crosslinking/IP followed by mass spectrometry shown in Figure 7G.

claim: The transient interaction between hTim8a and COX17 was not influenced by copper chelation with BCS.
source: The transient interaction between hTim8a and COX17 was not influenced by BCS suggesting that copper is not critical for their association.
evidence: This is demonstrated by crosslinking/IP experiments with BCS treatment shown in Figure 7I.

claim: There was a pronounced reduction in the interaction of hTim8aFLAG and COX17 with COX4 upon copper chelation.
source: However, there was a pronounced reduction in the interaction of hTim8aFLAG and COX17 with COX4 upon copper chelation (Figure 7I, compare lanes 5 and 6), showing the validity of the approach.
evidence: This is demonstrated by crosslinking/IP experiments with BCS treatment shown in Figure 7I.

claim: Pre-incubation of mitochondria with GSH significantly compromised the interaction of hTim8aFLAG with COX17.
source: Importantly, pre-incubation of mitochondria with GSH significantly compromised the interaction of hTim8aFLAG with COX17 (Figure 7I, compare lanes 4 and 5), indicating that the oxidation status of the cysteine residues in these proteins is crucial to maintain their association.
evidence: This is demonstrated by crosslinking/IP experiments with GSH treatment shown in Figure 7I.

claim: The oxidation status of the cysteine residues in hTim8a and COX17 is crucial to maintain their association.
source: Importantly, pre-incubation of mitochondria with GSH significantly compromised the interaction of hTim8aFLAG with COX17 (Figure 7I, compare lanes 4 and 5), indicating that the oxidation status of the cysteine residues in these proteins is crucial to maintain their association.
evidence: This is inferred from the GSH treatment experiment shown in Figure 7I.

claim: hTim8a interacts with a collection of Complex IV assembly factors and subunits and this interaction is enhanced under high respiratory demand.
source: These data show that hTim8a interacts with a collection of Complex IV assembly factors and subunits and this interaction is enhanced under high respiratory demand, suggesting a novel role of hTim8a in the maturation of Complex IV, analagous to that of an assembly factor.
evidence: This is demonstrated by crosslinking/IP experiments shown in Figure 7.

claim: hTim8a has a novel role in the maturation of Complex IV, analogous to that of an assembly factor.
source: These data show that hTim8a interacts with a collection of Complex IV assembly factors and subunits and this interaction is enhanced under high respiratory demand, suggesting a novel role of hTim8a in the maturation of Complex IV, analagous to that of an assembly factor.
evidence: This is inferred from the crosslinking/IP data showing interactions with Complex IV components.

claim: ROS levels were significantly elevated in SH-SY5Y cells lacking hTim8a compared to controls.
source: To assess oxidative stress in cells lacking hTim8a, cells were either left untreated or pre-treated with the oxidative stress inducing agent, menadione prior to H2O2 ROS level measurement. ROS levels were significantly elevated compared to controls in both SH-SY5Y (Figure 8A) and HEK293 cells lacking hTim8a, but not hTim8b (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: This is demonstrated by ROS assays shown in Figure 8A.

claim: ROS levels were significantly elevated in HEK293 cells lacking hTim8a, but not hTim8b.
source: ROS levels were significantly elevated compared to controls in both SH-SY5Y (Figure 8A) and HEK293 cells lacking hTim8a, but not hTim8b (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: This is demonstrated by ROS assays shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Challenging cells with menadione alone increased the apoptotic vulnerability of hTim8a-deficient SH-SY5Y cells.
source: Challenging the cells with menadione alone increased the apoptotic vulnerability of hTim8a-deficient SH-SY5Y cells (Figure 8B), indicating that ROS accumulation and an impaired capacity to deal with ROS are contributing to the heightened apoptotic vulnerability in hTim8aMUT SH cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated by apoptosis assays with menadione treatment shown in Figure 8B.

claim: ROS accumulation and an impaired capacity to deal with ROS are contributing to the heightened apoptotic vulnerability in hTim8aMUT SH cells.
source: Challenging the cells with menadione alone increased the apoptotic vulnerability of hTim8a-deficient SH-SY5Y cells (Figure 8B), indicating that ROS accumulation and an impaired capacity to deal with ROS are contributing to the heightened apoptotic vulnerability in hTim8aMUT SH cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the menadione treatment experiments shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Attenuating the oxidative stress in hTim8aMUT SH-SY5Y cells with Vitamin E reduces the levels of cytochrome c.
source: Attenuating the oxidative stress in hTim8aMUT SH-SY5Y cells with the anti-oxidants Vitamin E (α-tocopherol; Vit E) that prevents lipid peroxidation in cellular membranes (Traber and Atkinson, 2007; Traber and Stevens, 2011), reduces the levels of cytochrome c (Figure 8C)
evidence: This is demonstrated by western blot analysis with Vitamin E treatment shown in Figure 8C and supported by citations to Traber and Atkinson, 2007 and Traber and Stevens, 2011.

claim: Vitamin E treatment lowers the sensitivity of hTim8aMUT SH cells to apoptotic insult.
source: Attenuating the oxidative stress in hTim8aMUT SH-SY5Y cells with the anti-oxidants Vitamin E (α-tocopherol; Vit E) that prevents lipid peroxidation in cellular membranes (Traber and Atkinson, 2007; Traber and Stevens, 2011), reduces the levels of cytochrome c (Figure 8C) and was accompanied by lowered sensitivity of these cells to apoptotic insult (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by apoptosis assays with Vitamin E treatment shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Vitamin E treatment did not restore the abundance of Complex IV subunits and assembly factors, MTCO1 and COX17.
source: Although Vitamin E treatment did not restore the abundance of Complex IV subunits and assembly factors, MTCO1 and COX17 (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B), or monomeric Complex IV (Figure 8—figure supplement 1C and D)
evidence: This is demonstrated by western blot and BN-PAGE analysis with Vitamin E treatment shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1B-D.

claim: Vitamin C treatment did not have an effect on apoptotic sensitivity in hTim8aMUT SH cells.
source: we did not observe any effect with Vitamin C, which functions as a water-soluble antioxidant (Traber and Stevens, 2011), suggesting a Vitamin E specific response.
evidence: This is demonstrated by apoptosis assays with Vitamin C treatment shown in Figure 8D and supported by a citation to Traber and Stevens, 2011.

claim: Cells lacking COX17 had increased protein levels of cytochrome c.
source: Given the common impact on COX17 across our cell models we depleted SH-SY5Y cells of COX17 via siRNA and monitored the cellular consequences. Like SH-SY5Y cells lacking hTim8a, cells lacking COX17 had increased protein levels of cytochrome c (Figure 9A)
evidence: This is demonstrated by western blot analysis of COX17 knockdown cells shown in Figure 9A.

claim: Cells lacking COX17 had destabilization of Complex IV on BN-PAGE.
source: Like SH-SY5Y cells lacking hTim8a, cells lacking COX17 had increased protein levels of cytochrome c (Figure 9A); destablisation of Complex IV on BN-PAGE (Figure 9B)
evidence: This is demonstrated by BN-PAGE analysis of COX17 knockdown cells shown in Figure 9B.

claim: Cells lacking COX17 had reduced mitochondrial membrane potential.
source: Like SH-SY5Y cells lacking hTim8a, cells lacking COX17 had increased protein levels of cytochrome c (Figure 9A); destablisation of Complex IV on BN-PAGE (Figure 9B); reduced mitochondrial membrane potential (Figure 9C)
evidence: This is demonstrated by TMRM uptake assays of COX17 knockdown cells shown in Figure 9C.

claim: Cells lacking COX17 had enhanced sensitivity to intrinsic cell death.
source: Like SH-SY5Y cells lacking hTim8a, cells lacking COX17 had increased protein levels of cytochrome c (Figure 9A); destablisation of Complex IV on BN-PAGE (Figure 9B); reduced mitochondrial membrane potential (Figure 9C); enhanced sensitivity to intrinsic cell death (Figure 9D and E)
evidence: This is demonstrated by apoptosis assays of COX17 knockdown cells shown in Figures 9D and E.

claim: Cells lacking COX17 had oxidative stress that could initiate apoptosis.
source: Like SH-SY5Y cells lacking hTim8a, cells lacking COX17 had increased protein levels of cytochrome c (Figure 9A); destablisation of Complex IV on BN-PAGE (Figure 9B); reduced mitochondrial membrane potential (Figure 9C); enhanced sensitivity to intrinsic cell death (Figure 9D and E); and oxidative stress (Figure 9F) that could initiate apoptosis (Figure 9G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ROS and apoptosis assays of COX17 knockdown cells shown in Figures 9F and G.

claim: Re-expression of COX17FLAG in hTim8MUT SH cells reverted mitochondrial membrane potential defects.
source: Indeed, the parameters measured: (i) mitochondrial membrane potential (Figure 9I); (ii) apoptosis sensitivity following STS treatment (Figure 9J); (iii) oxidative stress (Figure 9K); and (iv) apoptosis sensitivity due to oxidative stress (Figure 9L) were all reverted in hTim8MUT SH cells expressing the COX17 (Figure 9H)
evidence: This is demonstrated by TMRM uptake assays shown in Figure 9I.

claim: Re-expression of COX17FLAG in hTim8MUT SH cells reverted apoptosis sensitivity following STS treatment.
source: Indeed, the parameters measured: (i) mitochondrial membrane potential (Figure 9I); (ii) apoptosis sensitivity following STS treatment (Figure 9J); (iii) oxidative stress (Figure 9K); and (iv) apoptosis sensitivity due to oxidative stress (Figure 9L) were all reverted in hTim8MUT SH cells expressing the COX17 (Figure 9H)
evidence: This is demonstrated by apoptosis assays shown in Figure 9J.

claim: Re-expression of COX17FLAG in hTim8MUT SH cells reverted oxidative stress.
source: Indeed, the parameters measured: (i) mitochondrial membrane potential (Figure 9I); (ii) apoptosis sensitivity following STS treatment (Figure 9J); (iii) oxidative stress (Figure 9K); and (iv) apoptosis sensitivity due to oxidative stress (Figure 9L) were all reverted in hTim8MUT SH cells expressing the COX17 (Figure 9H)
evidence: This is demonstrated by ROS assays shown in Figure 9K.

claim: Re-expression of COX17FLAG in hTim8MUT SH cells reverted apoptosis sensitivity due to oxidative stress.
source: Indeed, the parameters measured: (i) mitochondrial membrane potential (Figure 9I); (ii) apoptosis sensitivity following STS treatment (Figure 9J); (iii) oxidative stress (Figure 9K); and (iv) apoptosis sensitivity due to oxidative stress (Figure 9L) were all reverted in hTim8MUT SH cells expressing the COX17 (Figure 9H)
evidence: This is demonstrated by apoptosis assays with menadione treatment shown in Figure 9L.

claim: Defective Complex IV and the corresponding oxidative stress is initiating downstream sensitization of SH-SY5Y cells lacking hTim8a to death.
source: suggesting that defective Complex IV and the corresponding oxidative stress is initiating downstream sensitisation of SH-SY5Y cells lacking hTim8a to death.
evidence: This is inferred from the COX17 complementation experiments shown in Figure 9.

claim: Comparative analysis of neuronal-like and non-neuronal cells demonstrates the cell-specific function of the hTim8a and hTim8b isoforms.
source: This is the first study to comprehensively analyse the function of TIM chaperones across different human cell models and our findings highlight the functional specialisation of mitochondrial chaperones in different tissues. Comparative analysis of neuronal-like and non-neuronal cells demonstrates the cell-specific function of the hTim8a and hTim8b isoforms, with hTim8a function being critical for SH-SY5Y cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the differential effects of hTim8a and hTim8b loss in HEK293 and SH-SY5Y cells.

claim: hTim8a function is critical for SH-SY5Y cells.
source: Comparative analysis of neuronal-like and non-neuronal cells demonstrates the cell-specific function of the hTim8a and hTim8b isoforms, with hTim8a function being critical for SH-SY5Y cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the severe phenotypes observed in SH-SY5Y cells lacking hTim8a.

claim: Removal of hTim8a or hTim8b from both HEK293 or SH-SY5Y cells showed no impact to the biogenesis of the TIM22 complex or associated substrates, in particular hTim23.
source: While loss of hTim9 resulted in profound disruption of the TIM22-biogenesis pathway, removal of hTim8a or hTim8b from both HEK293 or SH-SY5Y cells showed no impact to the biogenesis of the TIM22 complex or associated substrates, in particular hTim23, whose perturbed import has been suggested to be the underlying basis of MTS (Rothbauer et al., 2001).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the import and BN-PAGE data shown in Figure 1 and supported by a citation to Rothbauer et al., 2001.

claim: hTim8a and hTim8b have evolved novel functions in human mitochondria in particular in the biogenesis of Complex IV.
source: Rather, our data suggests that hTim8a and hTim8b have evolved novel functions in human mitochondria in particular in the biogenesis of Complex IV.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the proteomics and functional data showing Complex IV defects.

claim: Complex IV dysfunction is associated with increased mitochondrial ROS and cellular toxicity.
source: Complex IV dysfunction is associated with increased mitochondrial ROS and cellular toxicity and causes a clinically heterogeneous variety of neuromuscular and non-neuromuscular disorders in childhood and adulthood and can result from either nuclear or mitochondrial mutations (Frazier et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a supporting citation to Frazier et al., 2019.

claim: Complex IV is unique among the respiratory chain complexes as it has tissue-specific subunit isoforms.
source: Complex IV is unique among the respiratory chain complexes as it has tissue-specific subunit isoforms, which are believed to have regulatory roles in adaptation of tissues to specific metabolic demands (Wallace and Fan, 2010).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a supporting citation to Wallace and Fan, 2010.

claim: hTim8a and hTim8b likely have multiple functions in mitochondrial biology.
source: Our crosslinking and IP data suggests that hTim8a and hTim8b likely have multiple functions in mitochondrial biology.
evidence: This is inferred from the crosslinking/IP data showing interactions with multiple protein complexes.

claim: Growth in glucose shows a predominant interaction of hTim8a with partner proteins hTim8b and hTim13, Complex IV related proteins, and key players involved in mitochondrial quality control.
source: Growth in glucose (low respiratory demand) shows a predominant interaction with: (i) partner proteins hTim8b and hTim13; (ii) Complex IV related proteins (Coa4, Coa7, cytochrome c and COX6B1) and key players involved in mitochondrial quality control including Opa1, the prohibitins and pGAM5.
evidence: This is demonstrated by crosslinking/IP followed by mass spectrometry shown in Figure 7G.

claim: hTim13 has been identified as a member of the SPY complex, an inner membrane regulatory hub.
source: Indeed, these interactions are evident in the literature with hTim13 coming down as a member of the SPY complex, an inner membrane regulatory hub (Wai et al., 2016)
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation to Wai et al., 2016.

claim: hTim8a and hTim13 immunoprecipitate with pGAM5.
source: and hTim8a and hTim13 immunoprecipitating with pGAM5 (Holze et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation to Holze et al., 2018.

claim: Under high respiratory demand, hTim8a shifts away from its interaction with hTim13 to exclusively engage in the Complex IV interaction network and mitochondrial quality control interactions.
source: Interestingly under high respiratory demand (growth on galactose) hTim8a shifts away from its interaction with hTim13 to exclusively engage in the Complex IV interaction network (including Coa4, Coa6, Coa7, COX41L and COX6B1) and mitochondrial quality control interactions.
evidence: This is demonstrated by crosslinking/IP followed by mass spectrometry shown in Figure 7G.

claim: Based on the lack of isolated defects in a specific Complex IV module in cells lacking hTim8a or hTim8b, the hTim8a/b are serving as assembly factors in Complex IV biogenesis, or have some regulatory role in chaperoning/guiding assembly factors to their place of action.
source: Based on the lack of isolated defects in a specific Complex IV module in cells lacking hTim8a or hTim8b, and the predominant engagement of hTim8a with proposed assembly factors, including COX17 we can only postulate at this stage that the hTim8a/b are serving as assembly factors in Complex IV biogenesis, or have some regulatory role in chaperoning/guiding assembly factors to their place of action.
evidence: This is speculation based on the experimental data.

claim: hTim8a could be a player that takes part in the redox-dependent modulation of COX17 for copper delivery to Complex IV.
source: Our identification of a copper-independent but redox-sensitive interaction between hTim8a and COX17 hints that hTim8a could be a player that take parts in the redox-dependent modulation of COX17 for copper delivery to Complex IV.
evidence: This is speculation based on the crosslinking/IP data shown in Figure 7I.

claim: Loss of functional COA6 results in a > 1.5 fold increase in the levels of COX17, hTim8a, hTim8b and hTim13.
source: In line with our observations, loss of functional COA6, which is thought to be required for delivery of Cu(I) to COX2 (Pacheu-Grau et al., 2015; Stroud et al., 2015), results in a > 1.5 fold increase in the levels of COX17, hTim8a, hTim8b and hTim13 (Stroud et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations to Pacheu-Grau et al., 2015 and Stroud et al., 2015.

claim: A similar pattern of Complex IV subunit turnover is observed in cells lacking COA6 to that observed in hTim8aKO SH-SY5Y cells.
source: Intriguingly, a similar pattern of Complex IV subunit turnover is observed in cells lacking COA6 to that observed in hTim8aKO SH-SY5Y cells (Stroud et al., 2015), suggesting the proteins impact Complex IV at a similar stage of its assembly.
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation to Stroud et al., 2015.

claim: Cell lines lacking hTim8a display heightened vulnerability to apoptotic induction due to oxidative stress.
source: Cell lines lacking hTim8a display heightened vulnerability to apoptotic induction due to oxidative stress.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the apoptosis and ROS data shown in Figures 3 and 8.

claim: The phenotype of heightened apoptotic vulnerability can be partially restored by the re-expression of COX17 in hTim8a deficient cells.
source: This phenotype can be partially restored by the re-expression of COX17 in these cells, strongly suggesting that oxidative stress is the driver of the observed apoptotic vulnerability.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the COX17 complementation experiments shown in Figure 9.

claim: Oxidative stress is the driver of the observed apoptotic vulnerability in cells lacking hTim8a.
source: This phenotype can be partially restored by the re-expression of COX17 in these cells, strongly suggesting that oxidative stress is the driver of the observed apoptotic vulnerability.
evidence: This is inferred from the COX17 complementation experiments shown in Figure 9.

claim: While cells lacking hTim8b have reduced levels of COX17, these cells do not display the same level of oxidative stress and are not as sensitive to apoptotic induction.
source: We cannot dismiss that there may be additional players, potential substrates of hTim8a, that could be contributing to this phenotype. Indeed, while cells lacking hTim8b have reduced levels of COX17 these cells do not display the same level of oxidative stress and ultimately are not as sensitive to apoptotic induction.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the ROS and apoptosis data shown in Figures 8 and 3.

claim: Cells lacking hTim8a are primed for cell death.
source: We propose that cells lacking hTim8a are primed for cell death, a term used to describe the proximity of cells to the apoptotic threshold (Ni Chonghaile et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the apoptosis sensitivity data and supported by a citation to Ni Chonghaile et al., 2011.

claim: The apoptotic sensitivity of cells lacking hTim8a was selectively rescued by treatment with the lipid-soluble anti-oxidant Vitamin E, but not the water-soluble Vitamin C.
source: The apoptotic sensitivity of cells lacking hTim8a was selectively rescued by treatment with the lipid-soluble anti-oxidant Vitamin E, but not the water-soluble Vitamin C.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the Vitamin E and C treatment experiments shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Vitamin E plays a major role in protecting membranes and nervous tissues from oxidative stress.
source: Vitamin E plays a major role in protecting membranes and nervous tissues from oxidative stress, where it scavenges peroxyl radical to maintain the integrity of long chain polyunsaturated fatty acids in cellular membranes (Traber and Atkinson, 2007; Traber and Stevens, 2011).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations to Traber and Atkinson, 2007 and Traber and Stevens, 2011.

claim: Lipid peroxidation is a potential oxidative pathway modulated upon hTim8a loss, leading to oxidative stress-induced apoptosis.
source: Our results therefore suggest lipid peroxidation as a potential oxidative pathway modulated upon hTim8a loss, leading to oxidative stress-induced apoptosis.
evidence: This is inferred from the Vitamin E rescue experiments.

claim: MTS is characterized in its end-stage by widespread and severe neuronal cell death in the central nervous system.
source: Importantly, MTS is characterized in its end-stage by widespread and severe neuronal cell death in the central nervous system (Hayes et al., 1998; Merchant et al., 2001; Tranebjaerg et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations to Hayes et al., 1998, Merchant et al., 2001, and Tranebjaerg et al., 2001.

claim: Cells lacking hTim8a have significant defects in glucose catabolism and mitochondrial metabolism.
source: In agreement with this, cells lacking hTim8a have significant defects in glucose catabolism and mitochondrial metabolism, both of which are evolutionarily linked to the regulation of cell death (King and Gottlieb, 2009).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the metabolomics data shown in Figure 5 and supported by a citation to King and Gottlieb, 2009.

claim: In SH-SY5Y cells, loss of hTim8a was associated with defects in glutamine catabolism and the operation of the malate-aspartate shunt.
source: In SH-SY5Y cells, loss of hTim8a was associated with defects in glutamine catabolism and the operation of the malate-aspartate shunt, which may underlie global changes in redox balance and ROS production, further contributing to the acute severity of loss of hTim8a on neuronal function (Mergenthaler et al., 2013).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the metabolomics and 13C-labeling data shown in Figure 5 and supported by a citation to Mergenthaler et al., 2013.

claim: Changes to the malate-aspartate shunt coincide with work showing that citrin and aralar1 are substrates of the hTim8a-hTim13 complex.
source: Changes to the malate-aspartate shunt coincides with work showing that citrin and aralar1, calcium-responsive aspartate-glutamate carriers that function in the malate-aspartate shuttle, are substrates of the hTim8a-hTim13 complex (Roesch et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation to Roesch et al., 2004.

claim: Loss of hTim8a in SH-SY5Y cells skewed the levels of epinephrine (elevated levels) and dopamine (lowered levels).
source: Strikingly, loss of hTim8a in SH-SY5Y also skewed the levels of epinephrine (elevated levels) and dopamine (lowered levels), two principal neurotransmitters, which are synthesised by the catecholamine biosynthesis pathway, a reaction unique and essential to the central nervous system and brain (Kobayashi, 2001).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the metabolomics data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2 and supported by a citation to Kobayashi, 2001.

claim: The data demonstrates a cell-specific function for hTim8a in the assembly of Complex IV in the SH-SY5Y cell model.
source: Our data demonstrates a cell-specific function for hTim8a in the assembly of Complex IV in the SH-SY5Y cell model, an in vitro model for neuronal cell function.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing Complex IV defects in SH-SY5Y cells lacking hTim8a.

claim: Previous work by Tranebjaerg et al. (2001) highlighted neuronal loss as a prominent feature in MTS patients.
source: Previous work by Tranebjaerg et al. (2001) highlighted neuronal loss as a prominent feature in MTS patients.
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation to Tranebjaerg et al., 2001.

claim: The study provides insight into the molecular features eliciting neuronal cell loss in MTS patients.
source: We now provide insight into the molecular features eliciting this cell loss and show that cells lacking hTim8a are sensitised to an oxidative stress induced intrinsic cell death.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing oxidative stress and apoptotic sensitivity in cells lacking hTim8a.

claim: The data highlights a strategy for early therapeutic intervention using Vitamin E for mitochondrial neuropathologies like MTS.
source: Importantly, our data highlights a strategy for early therapeutic intervention using Vitamin E for mitochondrial neuropathologies like MTS.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the Vitamin E rescue experiments shown in Figure 8.

claim: It would be appropriate to reclassify MTS from a secondary mitochondrial disease to a primary mitochondrial disease.
source: Given the role of hTim8a in Complex IV assembly we believe it would be appropriate to reclassify MTS from a secondary mitochondrial disease, to a primary mitochondrial disease.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the finding that hTim8a is involved in Complex IV assembly.
